meta.title: Mae Kampong Village Chiang Mai: Homestays, Waterfall & Transport
meta.description: Plan a trip to Mae Kampong Village, Chiang Mai: how to get there, where to stay, the 7-tier waterfall, Kew Fin sea of clouds and the best season to come.

meta.title: How to Get to Mae Kampong from Chiang Mai: Map & Road Tips
meta.description: Mae Kampong is 1–1.5 hours from Chiang Mai: self-drive via San Kamphaeng–Mae On, private car, day tours and public transport, plus parking, fuel and mountain-road tips.

transport.heading: Getting to Mae Kampong
transport.lead: The village sits in a valley in Huai Kaeo, Mae On district, at about 1,300 m. The last stretch is a winding mountain road — pick your transport before you set off.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get to Mae Kampong from Chiang Mai?
faqs.a: About 1 to 1.5 hours. The usual route is Chiang Mai → San Kamphaeng → Mae On → Huai Kaeo, ending with a long series of hairpin bends.

faqs.q: Is there public transport or a songthaew?
faqs.a: You can charter a car from Chiang Mai, or take public transport as far as the village entrance. Services are limited, so arrange your return in advance or join a round-trip day tour.

faqs.q: Anything to know before driving?
faqs.a: There is no fuel station and no public EV charger in the village — fill up or charge in San Kamphaeng or Mae On. Arriving before 09:00 makes parking at the village entrance much easier.

meta.title: Mae Kampong Village Accommodation & Homestays
meta.description: How to book a community homestay in Mae Kampong, what the rooms are like, when to reserve ahead, and how late you can eat if you are not staying overnight.

stay.heading: Where to stay
stay.lead: Rooms here are village homes registered with the community cooperative. Staying the night is what gets you the sea of clouds at dawn and a quiet valley after dark.

faqs.q: How do I book a homestay?
faqs.a: Homestays are registered with the village cooperative. They fill up fast in the cool season (November to February) and on weekends, so book ahead.

faqs.q: What are the rooms like?
faqs.a: Simple rooms with shared bathrooms, blankets and mosquito nets. The village is around 1,300 m up and usually 5–8 °C cooler than Chiang Mai city, so bring an extra layer for the night.

faqs.q: Can I eat in the village if I am not staying overnight?
faqs.a: Yes. Family kitchens and tea houses serve northern Thai dishes, highland oolong tea and coffee roasted in the village, mostly from morning to early evening — aim to eat before 18:00.

meta.title: Mae Kampong Attractions: Waterfall, Sea of Clouds & Coffee
meta.description: The seven-tier Mae Kampong Waterfall 1 km from the village, Kew Fin viewpoint at 1,517 m for the sea of clouds, tea terraces and village coffee experiences.

attractions.heading: Attractions & experiences
attractions.lead: The village is small. Three things are worth your time: the water at the falls, the sea of clouds at dawn, and the tea and coffee on the slopes.

faqs.q: How far is the walk to Mae Kampong Waterfall?
faqs.a: About 1 km from the village along a community nature trail, leading to a seven-tier waterfall. It is open 08:00–17:00 and the community charges a small fee — bring cash.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to see the sea of clouds?
faqs.a: Kew Fin viewpoint, about 3 km from the village inside Chae Son National Park at 1,517 m, gives a 360° sea of clouds at dawn. The cool season (November–February) is most reliable; be there before 06:30.

faqs.q: Is there a tea or coffee experience in the village?
faqs.a: Homestays and cafés serve highland oolong tea and coffee roasted in the village. Villagers once lived on pickled tea (Miang); the switch to high-value cool-season crops is what let the forest stay — that history is in the cup.

meta.title: Mae Kampong Opening Hours, Best Season & Itineraries
meta.description: The village is open all day and the waterfall 08:00–17:00. Compare the cool, hot and rainy seasons and pick a family or photography route.

plan.heading: Hours, seasons & itineraries
plan.lead: Decide what you came for — the clouds, the falls or a quiet village — then choose the season and the route.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Mae Kampong Village?
faqs.a: The village itself is open at any hour. The waterfall area is open 08:00–17:00, and the community fee is paid at the posted rate.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: November to February brings the clearest skies and the most reliable sea of clouds. June to October has the fullest waterfall but slippery trails. March to May can bring smoke from agricultural burning — check air quality before driving up.

faqs.q: How should I plan a day trip?
faqs.a: Stay in the village the night before, be at the viewpoint for the sea of clouds at dawn, walk to the waterfall in the morning, eat in the village at midday and head back in the afternoon — the mountain road is easier before dark.

about.label: About
about.heading: About Mae Kampong Village
about.locationHierarchy: Mae Kampong Village → Mae On → Chiang Mai → Thailand
about.lead: Mae Kampong is an old Lanna village set in a valley of Huai Kaeo, Mae On District, Chiang Mai Province, at about 1,300 m above sea level — cool year-round, with misty mornings.
about.paragraph1: The village is surrounded by rich pine and mountain forest, with highland strawberries, tea, cocoa and coffee, plus the Mae Kampong Waterfall flowing through the village. Community life is simple and in tune with nature.
about.paragraph2: Since the late 1990s, the village has developed Community-Based Tourism (CBT). Homestays and guides are fully run by villagers, with revenue feeding directly back into forest conservation, local healthcare, and education. Every step you take here supports the sustainable future of this centuries-old village.
about.quote: “When white mist rolls into the valley, the mountains become islands in a sea of clouds.”

history.label: History
history.heading: History & Significance of Mae Kampong Village
history.lead: Mae Kampong blends valley geography with Lanna heritage passed down through generations. Locals read the name as Mae ('mother' or 'river') plus Kampong ('stream' or 'weir') — 'Mother of the Kampong stream'. The brook still feeds the village, and its story is one of forest, faith and quiet self-reliance.

blocks.title: Lanna Migration (100+ years ago)
blocks.text: Lanna pioneers migrated from Chiang Saen and the Khun River area, settling along the Mae Kampong stream. They terraced rice fields and gathered forest products, naming the village after the stream that sustained them.

blocks.title: Miang: The Economic Lifeblood
blocks.text: What is Miang? It is a traditional Lanna fermented tea made from large tea leaves, chewed by locals for energy. Before modern tourism, gathering and fermenting Miang was the primary industry and the most important economic lifeline for Mae Kampong.

blocks.title: The Royal Project & Tea Culture (1970s–1980s)
blocks.text: For centuries, villagers made a living gathering wild tea leaves to make Miang (Lanna fermented tea). Later, inspired by King Bhumibol's initiative, the Teen Tok Royal Project Development Center introduced cool-climate crops — oolong tea and Arabica coffee — replacing slash-and-burn farming and letting the forest recover.

blocks.title: Community-Based Tourism (1996–present)
blocks.text: The village structured its community tourism, winning Thailand Tourism Awards and becoming a model for CBT in Thailand. The core lies in the 'Community Cooperative Model' — tourism revenue is not just for individuals, but is distributed to community funds, forest fire prevention teams, and pension funds, truly achieving sustainable ecological and economic development.

blocks.title: Name & Living Traditions
blocks.text: The village keeps a Lanna rhythm through the year. Cool season (Nov–Feb) brings the famous sea of clouds and the homestay high season, with Loy Krathong and New Year merit-making at the stream shrine. Each year households still leave offerings of flowers and incense to the stream spirit for rain and calm.

legend.title: Local legend
legend.text: Locals say that on calm mornings the mist rolls into the valley until it becomes a 'sea of clouds', and they believe that those who arrive at dawn will find a rare peace. They also believe the Mae Kampong stream is guarded by a village spirit, and on festival days and at the start of the rainy season leave flowers and incense at the water's edge to ask for rain and calm.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: At over 1,300 m, Mae Kampong is several degrees cooler than Chiang Mai — still fresh even in summer.

faqs.q: Where is Mae Kampong Village located?
faqs.a: Mae Kampong Village is located in Huai Kaeo, Mae On District, Chiang Mai Province, Thailand (postal code 50130), about a 1–1.5 hour drive east of Chiang Mai city.

faqs.q: Is Mae Kampong free to visit?
faqs.a: Yes, Mae Kampong Village is a public village and is free to visit year-round; only the community waterfall charges a small maintenance fee.

faqs.q: How far is Mae Kampong from Chiang Mai?
faqs.a: About a 1–1.5 hour drive, east of Chiang Mai.

faqs.q: When is the sea of clouds best?
faqs.a: At dawn 06:00–08:00, especially in the cool season (Nov–Feb).

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee?
faqs.a: The village is free; the waterfall charges a small community fee — bring cash.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight?
faqs.a: Yes — several community homestays; booking ahead is recommended.

faqs.q: Is it suitable for seniors and children?
faqs.a: Most trails are short and flat, good for all ages, but watch for slipperiness at dawn.

faqs.q: What is Mae Kampong famous for?
faqs.a: Highland oolong tea and Arabica coffee, the seven-tier Mae Kampong Waterfall, community homestays and the dawn 'sea of clouds' rolling over the valley.

faqs.q: Is there parking and are there public restrooms?
faqs.a: Yes. Open-air parking lots sit at the village entrance and along the main lane, and public restrooms are available near the car park and at the waterfall entrance. Homestays and tea houses also let visitors use their facilities.

faqs.q: Can I refuel or charge an electric car in the village?
faqs.a: No. There is no fuel station and no public EV charger in Mae Kampong. Refuel or recharge in San Kamphaeng or Mae On before the mountain climb.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day to visit Mae Kampong?
faqs.a: The first two hours after sunrise. That is when the valley fills with mist, the light on the tea terraces is softest, and the village is still quiet.

science.label: Science & responsibility
science.heading: Why Mae Kampong looks the way it does
science.lead: The mist, the cool air and the tea on the hillsides are all connected. Four short explanations for curious visitors.

cards.title: Why the valley fills with cloud
cards.text: On clear, windless nights the ground loses heat by radiation. Cold air is heavier, so it slides down the slopes and pools in the valley. Once the air near the ground cools to its dew point, water vapour condenses into tiny droplets — fog. Seen from a ridge above, that fog is exactly what visitors call a sea of clouds.

cards.title: Why it is cooler than Chiang Mai
cards.text: Air temperature falls by roughly 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m of altitude. Mae Kampong sits at about 1,300 m while Chiang Mai city is near 300 m, which is why the village is typically 5–8 °C cooler — and why dawns feel genuinely cold.

cards.title: Where the stream comes from
cards.text: The Mae Kampong stream is fed by rainfall captured in the watershed forest above the village. Moss, leaf litter and tree roots slow the water down and release it gradually through the year rather than in one runoff surge. Protecting that forest is what keeps the village water supply stable.

cards.title: From Miang to tea: an economy that regrew a forest
cards.text: Villagers once relied on Miang — tea leaves fermented and chewed — alongside shifting cultivation. High-value cool-climate crops introduced with royal project support gave households an alternative that keeps trees on the hillside, and community-based tourism gave visitors a reason to keep the forest standing.

responsibility: Stay on marked trails — the forest floor is a living soil layer, not a path
Carry out everything you carry in; there is no collection service on the trail
Keep noise low at dawn: the valley is a home before it is a viewpoint
Ask before photographing residents, their homes or their work
Pay community fees as posted — they fund trail upkeep and the village welfare fund
etiquette: Dress modestly in the village and when visiting the temple
Remove shoes before stepping into a home or onto a raised wooden platform
Accept tea with both hands; a small refusal is polite, a warm thank-you is better
Choose community-run homestays and guides so the income stays in the village
